docs.title: WGU Introduction to IT — Day 1 Study Guide
Today's Goal
docs.text:
By the end of Day 1, you should be able to:

  1. Define Information Technology (IT).
  2. Explain the difference between IT and Information Systems (IS).
  3. Identify the major components of an organization's IT environment.
  4. Explain how people, processes, technology, and data work together.
  5. Distinguish between hardware, software, data, and networks.
  6. Explain why IT is important to organizations.
  7. Describe the basic role of an IT department.

docs.title: 1. What Is Information Technology?
docs.text:
At its simplest:

Information Technology is the use of technology to create, store, process, transmit, protect, and manage information.

IT includes much more than computers.

An organization's IT environment can include:

  • Computers
  • Servers
  • Networks
  • Cloud infrastructure
  • Applications
  • Databases
  • Cybersecurity systems
  • Mobile devices
  • Data
  • Software development
  • IT support
  • Identity and access management
  • Artificial intelligence

Think of IT as an ecosystem, rather than a collection of individual technologies.

docs.title: 2. IT vs. Information Systems
docs.text: These terms are related and sometimes used interchangeably, but there's a useful distinction.

docs.title: Information Technology
docs.text:
Focuses primarily on the technology used to handle information.

Examples:

  • Servers
  • Networks
  • Databases
  • Software
  • Cloud platforms
  • Security systems

docs.title: Information Systems
docs.text:
A broader concept that includes:

People + processes + data + technology

An information system exists to accomplish some organizational purpose.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Imagine a hospital's patient scheduling system.

The IT includes:

  • Application servers
  • Database
  • Network
  • Application software
  • Security controls

The information system includes those technologies plus:

  • Scheduling employees
  • Patients
  • Doctors
  • Scheduling procedures
  • Business rules
  • Patient data
  • Policies

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text: Technology is a component of an information system.

docs.title: 3. The Four Major Components
docs.text: A useful model for understanding information systems is:

docs.title: People
docs.text:
The humans involved.

Examples:

  • Employees
  • Customers
  • IT administrators
  • Developers
  • Managers
  • Analysts

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
The activities and rules used to accomplish something.

Examples:

  • How an employee requests access
  • How a customer places an order
  • How backups are performed
  • How software gets deployed

docs.title: Technology
docs.text:
The tools that support the process.

Examples:

  • Computers
  • Applications
  • Databases
  • Networks
  • Servers
  • Cloud platforms

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The information being collected, stored, processed, or transmitted.

Examples:

  • Customer records
  • Financial transactions
  • Product information
  • Employee records
  • Healthcare information

docs.title: The key idea
docs.text:
These components work together.

For example:

Customer

↓

Places order

↓

E-commerce application

↓

Database

↓

Payment system

↓

Order fulfillment

The technology enables the process, but people and business processes determine what the system actually needs to accomplish.

docs.title: 4. Hardware
docs.text:
Hardware is the physical equipment used by an IT system.

Examples:

  • Laptop
  • Desktop
  • Smartphone
  • Server
  • Hard drive
  • SSD
  • Router
  • Network switch
  • Monitor
  • Printer

A simple way to remember it:

Hardware = something you can physically touch.

docs.title: 5. Software
docs.text:
Software consists of the programs and instructions that tell hardware what to do.

Examples:

  • Windows
  • macOS
  • Microsoft Excel
  • Web browsers
  • Database software
  • Mobile applications
  • Enterprise applications

A useful distinction:

docs.title: System Software
docs.text:
Helps operate the computer itself.

Example:

Windows

docs.title: Application Software
docs.text:
Helps the user accomplish a specific task.

Examples:

Excel Salesforce Chrome A healthcare analytics application

docs.title: 6. Data
docs.text:
Data is one of the most important assets in modern organizations.

Consider a healthcare supply-chain company.

It might have data about:

  • Customers
  • Hospitals
  • Products
  • Vendors
  • Purchases
  • Prices
  • Contracts
  • Savings opportunities

Raw data can be processed to produce useful information.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Raw data:

Product A — $10.00 Product A — $12.00 Product A — $9.00

Processed/analyzed information:

"Hospital A is paying 20% more than the organization's benchmark price for Product A."

That's where IT starts creating business value.

docs.title: 7. Networks
docs.text:
A network allows computers and other devices to communicate.

Examples:

  • Home Wi-Fi
  • Corporate networks
  • The Internet
  • Cellular networks
  • Cloud networks

A very simple model:

Device A

↓

Network

↓

Device B

The network doesn't necessarily store or process the information itself. Its primary job is to allow communication between systems.

We'll study networking much more deeply in Week 2.

docs.title: 8. Applications
docs.text:
An application is software designed to perform tasks for users or other systems.

Examples:

  • Banking application
  • Hospital scheduling application
  • CRM
  • Accounting system
  • Analytics platform
  • Email application

Applications often sit in the middle of the IT ecosystem.

For example:

User

↓

Application

↓

API

↓

Database

↓

Infrastructure

We'll eventually break down each of those components.

docs.title: 9. What Does an IT Department Do?
docs.text: An IT organization can have many responsibilities.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Maintains:

  • Servers
  • Networks
  • Cloud environments
  • Storage

docs.title: Application Development
docs.text: Builds and maintains software.

docs.title: Database/Data
docs.text:
Manages:

  • Databases
  • Data pipelines
  • Data quality
  • Analytics infrastructure

docs.title: Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Protects:

  • Systems
  • Networks
  • Applications
  • Data
  • Users

docs.title: IT Operations
docs.text: Keeps systems functioning.

docs.title: Help Desk / Support
docs.text: Helps users solve technology problems.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Determines how technology systems should fit together.

docs.title: 10. IT as a Business Function
docs.text:
One of the most important ideas for this course:

IT exists to support organizational objectives.

Technology isn't valuable simply because it's technologically impressive.

Consider two projects:

docs.title: Project A
docs.text: Company spends $2 million building an advanced AI system that nobody uses.

docs.title: Project B
docs.text:
Company spends $100,000 automating a manual process that saves employees 20,000 hours per year.

Project B may produce substantially more business value.

This is why IT and business strategy are increasingly interconnected.

docs.title: 11. The IT Ecosystem
docs.text:
Here's the mental model I want you to start developing.

```text BUSINESS │ ▼ PEOPLE │ ▼ PROCESSES │ ▼ APPLICATIONS / \ / \ ▼ ▼ DATA APIs │ │ └──────┬──────┘ ▼ NETWORK │ ▼ SERVERS / CLOUD │ ▼ HARDWARE

      ┌─────────────────────┐
      │     SECURITY        │
      │ protects everything │
      └─────────────────────┘

docs.title: WGU Introduction to IT — Day 2 Study Guide
Topic: Computer Hardware, Software & Operating Systems
Today's Goal
docs.text:
By the end of Day 2, you should be able to:

  1. Identify the major components of a computer system.
  2. Explain the purpose of the CPU, RAM, storage, motherboard, and GPU.
  3. Distinguish between volatile and non-volatile memory.
  4. Explain the difference between HDD and SSD storage.
  5. Explain what an operating system does.
  6. Distinguish between system software and application software.
  7. Explain the basic relationship between hardware, the operating system, and applications.
  8. Explain the difference between a client and a server.
  9. Understand why organizations use servers rather than relying only on individual computers.

docs.title: 1. The Basic Computer Model
docs.text:
At the most basic level, a computer system does four things:

Input → Processing → Storage → Output

For example, imagine entering a number into a calculator application.

Input

You type:

25 + 75

↓

Processing

The CPU performs the calculation.

↓

Storage

The computer may temporarily hold the information in memory.

↓

Output

The application displays:

100

Almost every computer system can be understood through some variation of this model.

docs.title: 2. Hardware vs. Software
docs.text:
Remember from Day 1:

Hardware is the physical equipment.

Software is the instructions that tell the hardware what to do.

For example:

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
• CPU
  • RAM
  • SSD
  • Keyboard
  • Monitor
  • Motherboard

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• Windows
  • macOS
  • Linux
  • Microsoft Excel
  • Chrome
  • Database applications

The two depend on each other.

You can't run Excel without hardware.

But hardware without software isn't particularly useful as a general-purpose computer.

docs.title: 3. The CPU — Central Processing Unit
docs.text:
The CPU is often described as the "brain" of the computer.

That's a useful beginner analogy, although it isn't technically perfect.

The CPU executes instructions and performs calculations.

For example, when software tells the computer:

"Add these two numbers."

The CPU performs the underlying operations necessary to accomplish that instruction.

docs.title: Important CPU concepts
docs.text:
You may encounter:

  • CPU cores
  • Clock speed
  • Threads
  • Cache

For this course, focus primarily on:

The CPU executes instructions and performs processing.

docs.title: 4. CPU Cores
docs.text:
Modern CPUs commonly have multiple cores.

For example:

  • 2-core CPU
  • 4-core CPU
  • 8-core CPU
  • 16-core CPU

A core can execute instructions.

Multiple cores allow a CPU to work on multiple tasks concurrently.

docs.title: Simple analogy
docs.text: Imagine a restaurant kitchen.

docs.title: One core
docs.text: One cook.

docs.title: Four cores
docs.text:
Four cooks.

More cooks can potentially handle more work simultaneously.

However, simply having more cores doesn't automatically make every application four times faster.

The software and workload matter.

docs.title: 5. RAM — Random Access Memory
docs.text:
RAM is the computer's short-term working memory.

When you open an application, the computer loads information into RAM so the CPU can access it quickly.

For example, imagine opening:

  • Chrome
  • Excel
  • Teams
  • Spotify

All of those programs need memory while they're running.

docs.title: RAM is volatile
docs.text:
This is an important term.

Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed.

If you turn off your computer, the information stored in RAM disappears.

Think:

RAM = temporary workspace

docs.title: 6. Storage
docs.text:
Storage is where information is kept for longer periods.

Examples:

  • SSD
  • HDD
  • USB drive
  • External hard drive

Unlike RAM, storage is generally non-volatile.

That means information remains when the computer is turned off.

For example:

You save a Word document.

The document is stored on the computer's storage device.

docs.title: 7. RAM vs. Storage
docs.text:
This distinction is extremely important.

RAM Storage Short-term working memory Long-term data storage Usually volatile Non-volatile Very fast Generally slower than RAM Used while programs are running Stores files and applications Contents disappear when power is lost Contents remain

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text:
Think of your desk.

RAM = what's currently on your desk

Storage = what's in your filing cabinet

Your desk is where you're actively working.

Your filing cabinet stores things for later.

docs.title: 8. HDD vs. SSD
docs.text: Two common types of storage are:

docs.title: HDD — Hard Disk Drive
docs.text: Uses spinning magnetic disks.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Usually inexpensive
  • Large capacities available

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Mechanical
  • Slower
  • More vulnerable to physical damage

docs.title: SSD — Solid State Drive
docs.text: Uses flash memory and has no moving mechanical disk.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Faster
  • More resistant to physical shock
  • Lower latency

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Historically more expensive per GB, although prices have decreased substantially

For modern computers, SSDs are extremely common.

docs.title: 9. The Motherboard
docs.text:
The motherboard is the primary circuit board connecting many of the computer's components.

It allows components such as:

  • CPU
  • RAM
  • Storage
  • GPU
  • Network hardware

to communicate with each other.

Think of it as the computer's central connection platform.

docs.title: 10. GPU — Graphics Processing Unit
docs.text:
The GPU is designed to perform graphics-related processing.

GPUs are especially important for:

  • Gaming
  • 3D graphics
  • Video processing
  • Scientific computing
  • Machine learning
  • AI workloads

Originally, GPUs were primarily associated with graphics.

Today, they are also extremely important for AI because they can perform many calculations simultaneously.

This is one of the first connections you'll encounter between traditional computer hardware and modern AI.

docs.title: 11. Input and Output Devices
docs.text: Computers need ways to interact with the outside world.

docs.title: Input Devices
docs.text:
Send information into the computer.

Examples:

  • Keyboard
  • Mouse
  • Microphone
  • Camera
  • Scanner
  • Touchscreen

docs.title: Output Devices
docs.text:
Present information from the computer.

Examples:

  • Monitor
  • Speakers
  • Printer
  • Projector

Some devices can perform both functions.

For example:

A touchscreen can display information and receive touch input.

docs.title: 12. What Is an Operating System?
docs.text:
The operating system, or OS, is the core system software that manages a computer's resources and provides an environment for applications to run.

Common operating systems include:

  • Microsoft Windows
  • macOS
  • Linux
  • Android
  • iOS

The operating system acts as an intermediary between applications and hardware.

A simplified model:

Application

↓

Operating System

↓

Hardware

For example:

You click "Print" in Microsoft Word.

Word doesn't need to directly control the printer's hardware.

Instead, it communicates through the operating system and associated drivers/services.

docs.title: 13. What Does an Operating System Do?
docs.text: An operating system performs many important functions.

docs.title: Resource Management
docs.text:
Manages:

  • CPU
  • RAM
  • Storage
  • Devices

docs.title: File Management
docs.text:
Provides ways to:

  • Create files
  • Open files
  • Rename files
  • Delete files
  • Organize files

docs.title: Process Management
docs.text: Controls running programs and processes.

docs.title: Device Management
docs.text: Helps software communicate with hardware devices.

docs.title: User Interface
docs.text:
Provides ways for users to interact with the computer.

Examples:

  • Windows desktop
  • macOS Finder
  • Linux desktop environments
  • Command-line interfaces

docs.title: 14. System Software vs. Application Software
docs.text: This distinction is worth memorizing.

docs.title: System Software
docs.text:
Supports the operation of the computer itself.

Examples:

  • Operating systems
  • Device drivers
  • System utilities

docs.title: Application Software
docs.text:
Helps users perform specific tasks.

Examples:

  • Microsoft Word
  • Excel
  • Chrome
  • Photoshop
  • Salesforce
  • Your company's analytics application

docs.title: Simple rule
docs.text:
Ask:

"Is this software primarily helping operate the computer, or helping the user accomplish a task?"

Operating system → System software

Excel → Application software

docs.title: 15. What Is a Server?
docs.text:
A server is a computer or software system that provides services or resources to other computers or systems.

The other systems are commonly called clients.

For example:

Client

Your laptop

↓

Network

↓

Server

Web server

The server might:

  • Deliver a webpage
  • Process an application request
  • Store files
  • Provide database services
  • Authenticate users

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
Usually requests or consumes a service.

Examples:

  • Laptop
  • Smartphone
  • Web browser
  • Mobile application

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
Provides a service.

Examples:

  • Web server
  • Database server
  • File server
  • Authentication server

The distinction is about role, not necessarily physical size.

A server doesn't have to be a giant machine sitting in a data center.

A server can be software running on a computer.

docs.title: 17. A Real-World Example
docs.text:
Imagine you open your company's analytics application.

You are using:

Your laptop

↓

Web browser

↓

Network

↓

Application server

↓

Database server

The laptop is acting as a client.

The application server provides the application.

The database server provides data.

This is the beginning of understanding client/server architecture.

docs.title: 18. Virtual Machines
docs.text:
You may encounter the term virtual machine (VM).

A virtual machine is a software-based computer that runs on physical hardware.

For example, one physical server might run:

```text Physical Server │ ├── Virtual Machine 1 │ └── Application Server │ ├── Virtual Machine 2 │ └── Database Server │ └── Virtual Machine 3 └── Web Server

docs.title: WGU Introduction to IT — Day 3 Study Guide
Day 3 Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

  1. Explain what a server is and how it differs from a typical client computer.
  2. Identify common types of servers and the services they provide.
  3. Explain what IT infrastructure means.
  4. Describe how servers, networks, storage, and applications work together.
  5. Explain virtualization.
  6. Explain what a virtual machine (VM) is.
  7. Explain why organizations use virtualization.
  8. Define cloud computing.
  9. Distinguish between on-premises and cloud infrastructure.
  10. Explain IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
  11. Describe how cloud computing changes IT management.
  12. Connect today's concepts to the Day 1 and Day 2 mental models.

docs.title: 1. The Big Picture
docs.text:
On Day 1, we looked at IT as an ecosystem:

People → Processes → Applications → Data → Technology

On Day 2, we zoomed in on an individual computer:

User → Application → Operating System → CPU/RAM/Storage → Hardware

Today we're going to zoom back out.

Most modern applications aren't running entirely on your laptop. When you use a website or enterprise application, your computer is usually communicating with other computers.

A simplified example:

Laptop → Network → Application Server → Database Server → Storage

This is where the concept of IT infrastructure becomes important.

docs.title: IT infrastructure
docs.text:
IT infrastructure is the collection of technology resources that allow an organization's applications and services to operate.

It can include:

  • Servers
  • Networks
  • Storage
  • Databases
  • Operating systems
  • Virtual machines
  • Cloud services
  • Data centers
  • Security systems
  • Backup systems
  • Monitoring systems
  • Identity and access systems

Think of infrastructure as the foundation that applications and business processes depend on.

docs.title: 2. What Is a Server?
docs.text:
A server is a computer or software system that provides a service or resource to other computers or applications.

The computer requesting the service is generally called the client.

A simple model is:

Client → Request → Server → Response → Client

For example, when you open a website:

  1. Your computer sends a request.
  2. A server receives the request.
  3. The server processes it.
  4. The server sends information back.
  5. Your browser displays the result.

The important thing to understand is that "server" describes a role.

A server doesn't necessarily have to look like a giant computer sitting in a data center.

A server could be:

  • A physical computer
  • A virtual machine
  • A cloud resource
  • A software application running on a computer

docs.title: 3. Client vs. Server
docs.text:
The simplest distinction is:

Client Server Requests services Provides services Usually used directly by a person Usually provides services to other systems Laptop Application server Smartphone Database server Web browser Web server Mobile app File server

For example:

When you use an analytics application:

Your laptop = client

Analytics application server = server

Database server = server

The client might request:

"Give me the savings opportunities for Company A."

The application server processes the request and may ask the database server for the required data.

docs.title: 4. A Server Doesn't Have to Be a Giant Computer
docs.text:
This is an important misconception to avoid.

You might imagine a server as a large physical machine like this:

Physical Server → Application

But modern IT environments often look more like:

Physical Server → Virtual Machine → Application

Or:

Cloud Provider → Virtual Server → Application

A virtual machine can perform the role of a server just like a physical computer can.

This becomes extremely important when we discuss virtualization.

docs.title: 5. Common Types of Servers
docs.text: Different servers perform different jobs.

docs.title: Web Server
docs.text:
A web server provides web content and handles web requests.

For example:

Browser → Web Server

The web server might return:

  • HTML
  • Images
  • CSS
  • JavaScript
  • Other web resources

docs.title: Application Server
docs.text:
An application server runs application logic.

For example, your financial analytics application might contain logic such as:

Find purchasing patterns that could generate savings.

The application server could perform that processing.

docs.title: Database Server
docs.text:
A database server stores and retrieves data.

For example:

Application → Database Server

The application might ask:

Give me all savings opportunities for CompanyID 123.

The database server retrieves the appropriate data.

docs.title: File Server
docs.text:
A file server provides centralized access to files.

Organizations might use file servers to store:

  • Documents
  • Spreadsheets
  • Reports
  • Shared files
  • Images

docs.title: Authentication Server
docs.text:
An authentication server helps determine whether a user is who they claim to be.

For example:

User → Login → Authentication System

The authentication system may verify:

  • Username
  • Password
  • MFA
  • Identity credentials

This connects directly to cybersecurity, which we'll study later.

docs.title: 6. What Is IT Infrastructure?
docs.text:
IT infrastructure is the underlying technology environment that supports an organization's applications and services.

Think about a hospital or healthcare company.

An application might appear simple to the user:

User → Healthcare Application

But underneath it could involve:

User → Laptop → Network → Application Server → Database → Storage → Backup → Security → Monitoring

All of those supporting components are part of the broader infrastructure.

docs.title: Infrastructure can include:
docs.text:
• Physical servers
  • Virtual machines
  • Networks
  • Storage
  • Databases
  • Operating systems
  • Data centers
  • Cloud services
  • Backup systems
  • Security systems
  • Monitoring tools
  • Identity systems

docs.title: 7. Infrastructure vs. Application
docs.text:
This distinction is worth learning.

An application performs a task for users.

Infrastructure provides the resources that allow the application to operate.

A useful analogy is a restaurant.

The restaurant's ordering application might be like the restaurant's menu and ordering process.

Infrastructure is more like:

  • Building
  • Electricity
  • Kitchen
  • Refrigeration
  • Plumbing
  • Equipment

The customer interacts primarily with the restaurant's services.

They don't necessarily think about the infrastructure making those services possible.

The same thing happens in IT.

Users interact with applications.

IT infrastructure supports those applications behind the scenes.

docs.title: 8. On-Premises Infrastructure
docs.text:
On-premises means an organization owns or directly operates its infrastructure in its own facilities or controlled environment.

For example:

Company → Data Center → Physical Servers

The organization might be responsible for:

  • Buying servers
  • Installing servers
  • Installing operating systems
  • Maintaining hardware
  • Replacing failed components
  • Managing networking
  • Managing storage
  • Managing databases
  • Managing security
  • Providing backups
  • Monitoring systems
  • Providing electricity and cooling

This can be expensive and complex.

docs.title: 9. What Is a Data Center?
docs.text:
A data center is a facility designed to house and operate IT infrastructure.

A data center may contain:

  • Servers
  • Storage systems
  • Network equipment
  • Power systems
  • Cooling systems
  • Physical security
  • Backup power
  • Fire suppression systems
  • Monitoring systems

Large organizations may operate their own data centers.

However, many organizations instead use cloud providers that operate enormous data centers on their behalf.

docs.title: 10. Why Do Organizations Use Servers?
docs.text: Servers provide several important advantages.

docs.title: Centralization
docs.text: Instead of storing everything on individual employee computers, organizations can centralize services.

docs.title: Shared Resources
docs.text: Many users can use the same application or service.

docs.title: Centralized Data
docs.text: Data can be stored in controlled systems rather than scattered across individual devices.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Organizations can apply centralized security controls.

docs.title: Management
docs.text: IT teams can manage systems centrally.

docs.title: Backup and Recovery
docs.text: Centralized systems can make backup and recovery easier to manage.

docs.title: Controlled Access
docs.text: Organizations can determine which users are allowed to access which systems and data.

docs.title: 11. What Is Virtualization?
docs.text:
Virtualization is the process of creating virtual versions of computing resources.

One of the most important examples is a virtual machine.

Instead of having:

Physical Server → One Computer

You can have:

Physical Server → VM 1 + VM 2 + VM 3 + VM 4

Each VM behaves like an independent computer.

This allows one physical machine to support multiple logical computers.

docs.title: 12. What Is a Virtual Machine?
docs.text:
A virtual machine (VM) is a software-based computer that runs on physical hardware.

A VM can have its own:

  • Operating system
  • CPU resources
  • RAM allocation
  • Storage
  • Applications
  • Network configuration

For example:

Physical Server

→ Windows VM → Linux VM → Database VM → Application VM

From the perspective of the software running inside the VM, it behaves much like a normal computer.

docs.title: 13. Why Use Virtualization?
docs.text: Virtualization provides several important advantages.

docs.title: Better Hardware Utilization
docs.text:
Without virtualization, a physical server might use only a fraction of its available resources.

Virtualization allows multiple workloads to share the same physical machine.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
Different VMs can operate independently.

A problem in one VM doesn't necessarily bring down every other VM.

docs.title: Flexibility
docs.text: IT teams can create, configure, move, and remove virtual machines more easily than physical machines.

docs.title: Cost Efficiency
docs.text:
Fewer physical servers can mean:

  • Less hardware
  • Less electricity
  • Less cooling
  • Less physical space
  • Less maintenance

This is one reason virtualization became such an important part of modern IT infrastructure.

docs.title: 14. Virtualization Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of virtualization as separating the logical computer from the physical hardware.

Instead of:

Physical Hardware → One Computer

you can have:

Physical Hardware → Virtualization → Multiple Virtual Computers

This creates an important abstraction between applications and physical hardware.

We'll come back to the concept of abstraction later.

docs.title: 15. What Is Cloud Computing?
docs.text:
Cloud computing means using computing resources and services provided over a network, typically the Internet.

Instead of an organization buying and operating every physical server itself, it can obtain computing resources from a cloud provider.

For example:

Company → Cloud Provider → Computing Resources

Common cloud providers include:

  • Microsoft Azure
  • Amazon Web Services (AWS)
  • Google Cloud

The cloud provider operates enormous amounts of infrastructure.

Organizations can consume those resources without necessarily owning the underlying physical hardware.

docs.title: 16. Cloud Does Not Mean "The Internet"
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

The Internet is a global network connecting computers and networks.

The cloud refers to computing resources and services delivered over networks.

For example:

Internet

= the network used to connect systems.

Cloud

= computing resources and services you access through that network.

Cloud providers can provide:

  • Computing
  • Storage
  • Databases
  • Networking
  • Security services
  • AI services
  • Monitoring
  • Backup services

docs.title: 17. On-Premises vs. Cloud
docs.text: Consider a company that needs a database.

docs.title: On-Premises
docs.text:
The company might:

  1. Buy a physical server.
  2. Install it in a data center.
  3. Install the operating system.
  4. Install database software.
  5. Configure storage.
  6. Configure networking.
  7. Maintain the hardware.
  8. Monitor the system.
  9. Handle backups.
  10. Replace failed components.

docs.title: Cloud
docs.text:
The company might instead:

  1. Select a cloud database service.
  2. Configure the database.
  3. Set permissions.
  4. Connect the application.
  5. Load the data.
  6. Monitor the service.

The cloud provider handles much of the underlying physical infrastructure.

However, cloud does not mean the customer has no responsibilities.

The customer may still be responsible for:

  • Data
  • Permissions
  • Application configuration
  • Database design
  • Business rules
  • Security settings
  • User access

This distinction becomes very important in cybersecurity.

docs.title: 18. Cloud Providers
docs.text: The three major cloud providers you'll commonly encounter are:

docs.title: Microsoft Azure
docs.text: Microsoft's cloud computing platform.

docs.title: Amazon Web Services
docs.text: Usually referred to as AWS.

docs.title: Google Cloud
docs.text:
Google's cloud computing platform.

All three provide many categories of services, including:

  • Compute
  • Storage
  • Databases
  • Networking
  • Security
  • AI
  • Analytics

You don't need to memorize specific services yet.

For now, understand the basic concept:

Cloud providers allow organizations to consume computing infrastructure and services without owning all of the physical infrastructure themselves.

docs.title: 19. IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service
docs.text:
IaaS stands for Infrastructure as a Service.

The provider gives you fundamental infrastructure resources.

Examples include:

  • Virtual machines
  • Storage
  • Networking
  • Computing resources

The customer generally has more responsibility.

A simplified model:

Provider: Physical hardware + virtualization

Customer: Operating system + applications + data

docs.title: Mental shortcut
docs.text: IaaS = "Give me infrastructure."

docs.title: 20. PaaS — Platform as a Service
docs.text:
PaaS stands for Platform as a Service.

The provider manages more of the underlying infrastructure and provides an environment where developers can build and run applications.

A simplified model:

Provider: Infrastructure + operating environment/platform

Customer: Application + data

docs.title: Mental shortcut
docs.text: PaaS = "Give me an environment where I can build and run my application."

docs.title: 21. SaaS — Software as a Service
docs.text:
SaaS stands for Software as a Service.

The provider delivers a completed software application.

The customer generally uses the application rather than managing the infrastructure underneath it.

Examples include:

  • Web-based email
  • CRM systems
  • Collaboration applications
  • Office applications
  • Enterprise software

docs.title: Mental shortcut
docs.text: SaaS = "Give me the software."

docs.title: 22. IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS
docs.text:
The easiest way to understand the three models is to think about who manages what.

Model Provider Manages Customer Manages IaaS Physical infrastructure, virtualization OS, applications, data PaaS Infrastructure + platform Application, data SaaS Infrastructure + platform + application Primarily configuration, users, data

The general pattern is:

IaaS → More customer responsibility

PaaS → Shared responsibility

SaaS → More provider responsibility

Don't worry about memorizing every boundary yet.

The important concept is that cloud services exist at different levels of abstraction.

docs.title: 23. Real-World Example: Financial Analytics Application
docs.text:
Imagine an organization using a financial analytics application.

The user might see:

User → Analytics Application

But behind the scenes:

User → Laptop → Internet/Corporate Network → Cloud Infrastructure → Application → Database → Data

The cloud environment might contain:

  • Virtual machines
  • Application servers
  • Database servers
  • Storage
  • Networking
  • Security systems
  • Monitoring
  • Backup systems

The user doesn't need to understand all of that to use the application.

This is one of the major benefits of abstraction.

docs.title: 24. What Is Abstraction?
docs.text:
Abstraction means hiding unnecessary implementation details so that users or systems can interact with something at a higher level.

Consider your laptop.

You might use:

Microsoft Word → Operating System → Hardware

You don't need to manually tell the CPU:

"Move these bytes from this memory location and perform this instruction."

The operating system and hardware abstraction handle those details.

Similarly, a cloud application might look like:

User → Application

But underneath:

Application → VM → Physical Server → Data Center

The user interacts with the higher-level abstraction.

docs.title: 25. Availability and Redundancy
docs.text:
Organizations often don't want an application to stop working because one server fails.

For example:

Application Server 1

Application Server 2

Application Server 3

If Server 1 fails, the other servers may continue serving users.

This is an example of redundancy.

Redundancy means having additional components or resources available so that the failure of one component does not necessarily cause the entire system to fail.

Redundancy can exist at many levels:

  • Multiple servers
  • Multiple network connections
  • Backup storage
  • Backup power
  • Replicated databases
  • Multiple data centers

This concept will become increasingly important when we study networking, cloud computing, and cybersecurity.

docs.title: 26. Infrastructure as a System
docs.text:
Let's combine everything we've learned.

A simplified modern application might look like this:

User

↓

Client Device

↓

Network

↓

Web/Application Server

↓

Database Server

↓

Storage

And underneath those systems:

Virtualization

↓

Physical Servers

↓

Data Center

Or, in a cloud environment:

Cloud Provider

↓

Compute / Database / Storage / Networking

↓

Application

↓

User

This is the architecture mindset we're beginning to develop.

docs.title: 27. Connecting Days 1, 2, and 3
docs.text: This is one of the most important sections of today's lesson.

docs.title: Day 1 — What Is IT?
docs.text:
We learned:

People + Processes + Applications + Data + Technology

We were looking at IT from an organizational perspective.

docs.title: Day 2 — What's Inside a Computer?
docs.text:
We learned:

Application → Operating System → CPU/RAM/Storage → Hardware

We were looking inside an individual computer.

docs.title: Day 3 — How Do Organizations Build Larger Systems?
docs.text:
Now we're looking at:

User → Client Device → Network → Application Server → Database Server → Storage

And underneath:

Physical Hardware → Virtualization → Virtual Machines → Cloud Services

We're moving from:

Individual Computer

to

IT Systems

to

IT Infrastructure

That progression is extremely important for the rest of this course.

docs.title: 28. Day 3 Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Server System that provides services or resources to other systems Client System that requests or consumes services Infrastructure Technology resources supporting applications and services Data Center Facility designed to house and operate IT infrastructure On-Premises Infrastructure owned/operated directly by an organization Virtualization Creating virtual versions of computing resources Virtual Machine (VM) Software-based computer running on physical hardware Cloud Computing Computing resources/services delivered over a network IaaS Infrastructure as a Service PaaS Platform as a Service SaaS Software as a Service Redundancy Additional resources that help tolerate failures Abstraction Hiding implementation details behind a simpler interface Web Server Provides web resources/services Application Server Runs application logic Database Server Stores and retrieves data File Server Provides centralized file storage/access Authentication Server Helps verify user identity

docs.title: 29. Exercise — Trace a Web Application
docs.text:
Choose a web application you use regularly.

It could be:

  • Your banking website
  • Salesforce
  • A healthcare application
  • Amazon
  • A news website
  • A project management tool
  • An analytics application

Then fill out:

Component Your Example User Client device Application Network Web/Application server Database Storage Virtualization likely involved? Cloud likely involved?

Then answer:

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What happens when the user clicks a button that requests new data?

Try to trace the request from:

User → Client → Network → Application → Database

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
What happens if the application server fails?

Would the entire application necessarily stop working?

Why or why not?

docs.title: Challenge Question
docs.text:
Which parts of this architecture are visible to the user?

Which parts are hidden by abstraction?

docs.title: 1. What is a server?
docs.text: A. A computer that must be physically located in a data center B. A computer with more than 32 GB of RAM C. A system that provides services or resources to other systems D. A computer running Windows Server

docs.title: 2. Which is most likely acting as a client?
docs.text: A. Database server B. Application server C. Laptop running a web browser D. Authentication server

docs.title: 3. What does IT infrastructure refer to?
docs.text: A. Only physical computers B. The underlying technology resources supporting applications and services C. Only cloud computing D. Only networking equipment

docs.title: 4. What is the primary purpose of a database server?
docs.text: A. Display webpages B. Authenticate users C. Store and retrieve data D. Provide electricity

docs.title: 5. What is virtualization?
docs.text: A. Converting physical files into digital files B. Using one physical computer to support multiple virtual computers C. Connecting computers to the Internet D. Encrypting network traffic

docs.title: 6. What is a virtual machine?
docs.text: A. A physical server with multiple processors B. A software-based computer running on physical hardware C. A cloud provider D. A database

docs.title: 7. Which is an advantage of virtualization?
docs.text: A. It eliminates the need for operating systems B. It guarantees that hardware can never fail C. It can improve utilization of physical hardware D. It removes the need for networks

docs.title: 8. What is cloud computing?
docs.text: A. Storing files exclusively on your laptop B. Connecting two computers with Ethernet C. Using computing resources and services delivered over a network D. Using only wireless Internet

docs.title: 9. Which cloud model provides basic infrastructure resources such as virtual machines and storage?
docs.text: A. SaaS B. PaaS C. IaaS D. DNS

docs.title: 10. Which cloud model provides a completed software application?
docs.text: A. IaaS B. PaaS C. SaaS D. VM

docs.title: 11. Which example best represents an on-premises environment?
docs.text: A. A company uses a SaaS CRM application B. A company operates physical servers in its own data center C. A company rents a cloud database D. An employee uses a web browser

docs.title: 12. Why might an organization use redundant application servers?
docs.text: A. To make computers physically smaller B. To eliminate databases C. To reduce the impact of a server failure D. To eliminate operating systems

docs.title: 13. Which server would most likely store and retrieve structured application data?
docs.text: A. Web server B. File server C. Database server D. Authentication server

docs.title: 14. What is abstraction?
docs.text: A. Removing hardware from a computer B. Hiding implementation details behind a simpler interface C. Encrypting data D. Replacing a physical server with a laptop

docs.title: 15. Which sequence best represents a simplified modern web application?
docs.text: A. Database → User → Client → Network → Application B. User → Client → Network → Cloud Infrastructure → Application → Database C. User → Database → Keyboard → Server D. Application → User → Storage → Network

docs.title: 1. C — System that provides services or resources
docs.text: A server is defined by the service it provides, not by its physical appearance.

docs.title: 2. C — Laptop running a web browser
docs.text: The laptop is requesting services from servers, making it a client.

docs.title: 3. B — Underlying technology resources supporting applications and services
docs.text: Infrastructure includes servers, networks, storage, virtualization, cloud services, and related systems.

docs.title: 4. C — Store and retrieve data
docs.text: That is the primary role of a database server.

docs.title: 5. B — One physical computer supporting multiple virtual computers
docs.text: This is the core concept behind virtualization.

docs.title: 6. B — Software-based computer running on physical hardware
docs.text: A VM behaves like a computer even though it is implemented through software.

docs.title: 7. C — Improve utilization of physical hardware
docs.text: Virtualization allows multiple workloads to share physical resources.

docs.title: 8. C — Computing resources and services delivered over a network
docs.text: Cloud computing isn't simply "the Internet." It involves computing resources and services delivered through networks.

docs.title: 9. C — IaaS
docs.text: Infrastructure as a Service provides fundamental computing infrastructure such as virtual machines, storage, and networking.

docs.title: 10. C — SaaS
docs.text: Software as a Service provides a completed software application.

docs.title: 11. B — Company operates physical servers in its own data center
docs.text: That is a classic example of on-premises infrastructure.

docs.title: 12. C — Reduce the impact of a server failure
docs.text: Redundant systems help maintain availability when individual components fail.

docs.title: 13. C — Database server
docs.text: Database servers specialize in storing and retrieving structured data.

docs.title: 14. B — Hiding implementation details behind a simpler interface
docs.text: Abstraction lets users interact with systems without needing to understand every underlying technical detail.

docs.title: 15. B — User → Client → Network → Cloud Infrastructure → Application → Database
docs.text: This represents a simplified version of a modern cloud-based application architecture.

docs.title: 33. Key Takeaway
docs.text:
The biggest idea from Day 3 is:

Applications depend on infrastructure.

A modern application isn't simply a piece of software sitting on someone's laptop.

It may depend on:

Users

↓

Client Devices

↓

Networks

↓

Application Servers

↓

Database Servers

↓

Storage

↓

Virtual Machines

↓

Physical Infrastructure

And increasingly:

Cloud Provider → Infrastructure → Virtualized/Managed Services → Applications → Users

docs.title: Your progression so far
docs.text:
Day 1 — What is IT?

People + Processes + Technology + Data

Day 2 — What's inside a computer?

Application + OS + CPU + RAM + Storage

Day 3 — How do organizations build larger systems?

Clients + Networks + Servers + Infrastructure + Virtualization + Cloud

You are now moving from understanding individual computers to understanding IT systems and infrastructure. That foundation will make the upcoming networking, databases, cybersecurity, and software-development topics much easier to understand.

docs.title: WGU Introduction to IT — Day 4 Study Guide
Topic
docs.text: Networks, IP Addresses, DNS, Protocols, and How Data Moves

docs.title: Day 4 Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

  1. Explain what a computer network is.
  2. Explain why organizations use networks.
  3. Distinguish between LANs, WANs, and the Internet.
  4. Explain the roles of switches and routers.
  5. Explain what an IP address is.
  6. Distinguish between private and public IP addresses.
  7. Explain the basic purpose of DNS.
  8. Explain what a protocol is.
  9. Identify common networking protocols such as HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, UDP, and DNS.
  10. Explain the difference between TCP and UDP at a high level.
  11. Explain the difference between a MAC address and an IP address.
  12. Trace a simplified request from a user's computer to a web server.
  13. Connect networking concepts to the servers, infrastructure, and cloud concepts from Day 3.

docs.title: 1. The Big Picture
docs.text:
On Day 3, we started looking at how computers communicate with servers:

User → Client → Network → Application Server → Database Server

Today we're going to focus on the network portion of that architecture.

A network allows computers and other devices to communicate with one another.

A simplified example:

Laptop → Wi-Fi → Router → Internet → Web Server

When you open a website, send an email, or use an enterprise application, information is traveling across one or more networks.

Networking is therefore one of the fundamental pieces connecting everything we've studied so far.

docs.title: 2. What Is a Computer Network?
docs.text:
A computer network is a collection of connected devices that can communicate and share resources.

Devices on a network might include:

  • Computers
  • Servers
  • Smartphones
  • Printers
  • Routers
  • Switches
  • IoT devices
  • Storage systems
  • Security devices

Networks allow devices to:

  • Exchange information
  • Access applications
  • Share files
  • Access databases
  • Access the Internet
  • Share printers
  • Communicate with servers

A network doesn't necessarily mean the Internet.

A small office network is a network.

A hospital's internal network is a network.

A home Wi-Fi network is a network.

The Internet is a network of networks.

docs.title: 3. Why Do Organizations Use Networks?
docs.text:
Networks allow organizations to connect people, systems, and resources.

Consider a healthcare organization.

An employee might need to access:

  • An internal application
  • A database
  • A file server
  • Email
  • A cloud application
  • The Internet
  • A printer

Without networking, these systems would largely exist in isolation.

Networking allows them to communicate.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A financial analyst might use:

Laptop → Corporate Network → Analytics Application → Database

The network is what allows those components to communicate.

docs.title: 4. LAN — Local Area Network
docs.text:
A LAN, or Local Area Network, connects devices within a relatively limited geographic area.

Examples include:

  • Home network
  • Office network
  • School network
  • Hospital building
  • Corporate building

A typical office might have:

Laptop

↓

Wi-Fi / Ethernet

↓

Switch

↓

Internal Network

The LAN allows devices within the organization to communicate.

docs.title: 5. WAN — Wide Area Network
docs.text:
A WAN, or Wide Area Network, connects networks across larger geographic areas.

For example, a company might have offices in:

  • Tennessee
  • Georgia
  • Texas
  • California

Those offices could have their own LANs.

A WAN can connect them:

Office LAN → WAN → Office LAN

WANs can span:

  • Cities
  • States
  • Countries
  • Continents

The Internet is an enormous interconnected collection of networks rather than simply one large LAN.

docs.title: 6. Internet vs. Network
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

A network is any connected group of devices.

The Internet is a massive global network of interconnected networks.

For example:

Your Home Network

↓

Internet Service Provider

↓

Internet

↓

Web Server

Your home network is only one small network participating in the larger Internet.

docs.title: 7. Wired vs. Wireless Networking
docs.text: Devices can connect to networks in different ways.

docs.title: Wired
docs.text:
A device connects using a physical cable.

Common example:

Ethernet cable

Advantages can include:

  • Consistent connection
  • High speeds
  • Low interference
  • Predictable performance

docs.title: Wireless
docs.text:
A device connects using radio signals.

The most common example is Wi-Fi.

For example:

Laptop → Wi-Fi → Wireless Access Point

Wireless networking provides mobility and convenience.

However, wireless connections can be affected by:

  • Distance
  • Walls
  • Interference
  • Signal strength
  • Congestion

docs.title: 8. What Is a Network Switch?
docs.text:
A network switch connects devices within a network and helps direct network traffic to the appropriate device.

Imagine an office with:

  • 20 laptops
  • 5 printers
  • 3 servers
  • 2 wireless access points

A switch can connect many of these devices to the same local network.

A simplified model:

Laptop A

↘

Switch

↗

Server

The switch helps determine where network traffic should go within the local network.

docs.title: 9. What Is a Router?
docs.text:
A router connects different networks and determines where network traffic should be sent.

For example:

Home Network → Router → Internet

The router connects your local network to another network.

In a corporate environment, routers can connect:

Corporate Network → Other Networks

The easiest distinction to remember:

Switches primarily connect devices within a network. Routers connect different networks.

This is a simplification, but it is a useful beginner mental model.

docs.title: 10. Switch vs. Router
docs.text: Device Primary Role Switch Connects devices within a network Router Connects different networks Wireless Access Point Provides wireless network connectivity

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A small office might look like:

Laptop

↓

Wi-Fi Access Point

↓

Switch

↓

Router

↓

Internet

Not every network will physically look exactly like this, but it provides a useful conceptual model.

docs.title: 11. What Is an IP Address?
docs.text:
An IP address is an address used to identify a device or network interface on an IP network.

Think of an IP address as a network address.

Just as a postal address helps identify where something should be delivered, an IP address helps network traffic determine where information should go.

An example IPv4 address looks like:

192.168.1.25

IPv4 addresses contain four numerical sections separated by periods.

Another example:

10.0.0.15

You don't need to memorize the mathematical details of IPv4 yet.

The important concept is:

Devices communicating over an IP network need addresses so traffic can be delivered to the correct destination.

docs.title: 12. IPv4 vs. IPv6
docs.text: There are two major versions of the Internet Protocol that you will encounter.

docs.title: IPv4
docs.text:
IPv4 uses addresses such as:

192.168.1.25

IPv4 has a limited number of available addresses.

docs.title: IPv6
docs.text:
IPv6 was developed in part because the world needed far more IP addresses.

An IPv6 address looks very different:

2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334

IPv6 addresses are much larger than IPv4 addresses.

For this course, you don't need to memorize IPv6 addressing rules.

Just remember:

IPv4 = older, widely used addressing system

IPv6 = newer addressing system with a vastly larger address space

docs.title: 13. Private vs. Public IP Addresses
docs.text: Not every IP address is directly reachable from the public Internet.

docs.title: Private IP Address
docs.text:
A private IP address is used within a private network.

Examples include addresses beginning with:

  • 10.x.x.x
  • 172.16.x.x through 172.31.x.x
  • 192.168.x.x

For example:

192.168.1.25

might identify your laptop within your home network.

docs.title: Public IP Address
docs.text:
A public IP address can be used for communication across the public Internet.

Your home network may have a public IP address assigned by your Internet service provider.

The basic concept is:

Private IP → Internal network

Public IP → Public Internet

docs.title: 14. What Is DNS?
docs.text:
One of the most important networking concepts you'll encounter is DNS.

DNS stands for:

Domain Name System

DNS translates human-friendly domain names into IP addresses.

For example, humans prefer to type:

example.com

Computers ultimately need network addresses such as:

93.184.216.34

DNS helps connect those two concepts.

A simplified process is:

Browser → DNS → IP Address

Then:

Browser → IP Address → Web Server

docs.title: 15. Why Do We Need DNS?
docs.text:
Imagine if you had to memorize the IP address of every website you used.

Instead of typing:

example.com

you would have to remember something like:

93.184.216.34

And if the website changed servers, the address might change.

DNS allows humans to use names while the network infrastructure works with addresses.

Think of DNS as somewhat like a phone book for domain names and IP addresses.

The analogy isn't perfect, but it's useful for understanding the basic purpose.

docs.title: 16. What Is a Protocol?
docs.text:
A protocol is a set of rules that defines how systems communicate.

Imagine two people trying to have a conversation.

They need some shared understanding about:

  • Language
  • Timing
  • Meaning
  • Structure

Computers need similar rules.

Networking protocols define things such as:

  • How information is formatted
  • How it is transmitted
  • How systems identify one another
  • How errors are handled
  • How communication begins and ends

Protocols allow devices built by different companies to communicate consistently.

docs.title: 17. Common Networking Protocols
docs.text:
There are many networking protocols.

You don't need to memorize all of them today.

Focus on these:

Protocol Basic Purpose HTTP Web communication HTTPS Secure web communication DNS Domain name resolution TCP Reliable transport of data UDP Faster, connectionless transport IP Addressing and routing network traffic

These protocols work at different layers of networking.

For now, focus on their purpose rather than memorizing every technical detail.

docs.title: 18. HTTP
docs.text:
HTTP stands for:

Hypertext Transfer Protocol

HTTP is one of the primary protocols used for communication between web browsers and web servers.

For example:

Browser → HTTP Request → Web Server

The server responds:

Web Server → HTTP Response → Browser

This is part of how web applications work.

docs.title: 19. HTTPS
docs.text:
HTTPS is HTTP with security provided through encryption using TLS.

You will commonly see:

https://

instead of:

http://

HTTPS helps protect information traveling between a client and a web server.

For example, when logging into a banking website, you don't want your username and password traveling across the network as readable text.

HTTPS helps protect that communication.

We'll study encryption and cybersecurity in more depth later.

For now:

HTTP = web communication

HTTPS = secure web communication

docs.title: 20. TCP
docs.text:
TCP, or Transmission Control Protocol, provides reliable communication between systems.

TCP is designed to make sure data is delivered reliably and in the correct order.

If some information is lost, TCP can help detect the problem and retransmit it.

Think of TCP as prioritizing:

Reliability

This is useful for things such as:

  • Web applications
  • File transfers
  • Email
  • Database communication

docs.title: 21. UDP
docs.text:
UDP, or User Datagram Protocol, takes a different approach.

UDP does not provide the same level of reliability and connection management as TCP.

That can make it faster and more efficient for certain types of communication.

UDP can be useful for:

  • Streaming
  • Voice communication
  • Online gaming
  • Real-time applications

For some applications, receiving information quickly is more important than guaranteeing that every packet arrives perfectly.

docs.title: Simplified comparison
docs.text:
TCP → Reliability

UDP → Speed / lower overhead

This is a simplification, but it is the right mental model for this stage of your learning.

docs.title: 22. TCP vs. UDP
docs.text:
TCP UDP Reliable Less reliable Connection-oriented Connectionless Tracks delivery Does not provide the same delivery guarantees Retransmits lost data Does not automatically retransmit in the same way More overhead Lower overhead Useful when accuracy matters Useful when speed matters

You don't need to memorize every technical difference yet.

The key idea is:

TCP emphasizes reliable delivery. UDP emphasizes speed and low overhead.

docs.title: 23. What Is a MAC Address?
docs.text:
A MAC address is a hardware/network interface identifier associated with a network interface.

A MAC address might look something like:

00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E

MAC addresses operate at a different level from IP addresses.

For now, think of the difference this way:

MAC address → identifies a network interface on the local network

IP address → provides an address used for communication across IP networks

This distinction will become clearer when you study networking more deeply.

docs.title: 24. MAC Address vs. IP Address
docs.text:
MAC Address IP Address Associated with network interface Network address Used primarily at the local network level Used for IP communication Typically represented in hexadecimal IPv4 commonly represented in decimal notation Example: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E Example: 192.168.1.25

Don't get too deep into this distinction yet.

At this stage, simply understand that MAC addresses and IP addresses serve different purposes.

docs.title: 25. How Does a Web Request Actually Work?
docs.text:
Let's put today's concepts together.

Imagine you type:

example.com

into your browser.

A simplified version of what happens is:

docs.title: Step 1 — You enter the domain
docs.text:
User → Browser

You type:

example.com

docs.title: Step 2 — DNS lookup
docs.text:
Your computer needs to determine which IP address corresponds to that domain.

Browser → DNS

DNS responds with an IP address.

docs.title: Step 3 — Network communication
docs.text:
Your computer sends traffic toward the destination IP address.

Laptop → Router → Internet

docs.title: Step 4 — Web server receives the request
docs.text:
The request reaches the appropriate web server.

Internet → Web Server

docs.title: Step 5 — Server processes request
docs.text: The server determines what information to return.

docs.title: Step 6 — Response returns
docs.text:
The server sends information back through the network.

Web Server → Internet → Router → Laptop

docs.title: Step 7 — Browser displays the result
docs.text: Your browser processes the response and displays the webpage.

docs.title: 26. Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Here's the complete simplified architecture:

User

↓

Browser

↓

DNS

↓

Network

↓

Router

↓

Internet

↓

Web/Application Server

↓

Database Server

↓

Storage

Notice how much of Day 3 is present.

We have:

  • Client
  • Network
  • Server
  • Database
  • Storage
  • Infrastructure
  • Cloud

Day 4 adds the networking concepts that connect those pieces.

docs.title: 27. The Network Is the Connector
docs.text:
This is perhaps the most important conceptual idea from today's lesson.

Consider the systems we've studied so far:

Client

Application Server

Database Server

Cloud Infrastructure

None of these systems are particularly useful to an organization if they cannot communicate.

The network connects them.

You can think of networking as the communication layer connecting the IT ecosystem.

docs.title: 28. Example: Healthcare Analytics Application
docs.text:
Let's apply this to a realistic enterprise example.

Imagine an analyst opens a healthcare supply-chain analytics application.

The analyst's computer might have:

Private IP: 192.168.1.25

The analyst opens the application in a browser.

The browser sends a request across the corporate network.

The traffic might travel through:

Laptop → Wi-Fi → Switch → Router → Corporate Network → Cloud → Application Server

The application server then requests data:

Application Server → Database Server

The database returns the requested information:

Database → Application Server

The application server sends the results back:

Application Server → Network → Analyst's Laptop

The analyst sees the results in the browser.

From the user's perspective, it feels like one application.

Technically, many systems are communicating behind the scenes.

docs.title: 29. Day 4 Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Network Connected devices that can communicate LAN Local Area Network WAN Wide Area Network Internet Global interconnected network of networks Switch Connects devices within a network Router Connects different networks IP Address Network address used for IP communication IPv4 Common version of IP using 32-bit addresses IPv6 Newer IP version with a much larger address space Private IP IP address used within a private network Public IP IP address used for communication over the public Internet DNS Resolves domain names to IP addresses Protocol Rules governing communication HTTP Web communication protocol HTTPS Secure web communication TCP Reliable transport protocol UDP Lower-overhead transport protocol MAC Address Network interface identifier Wi-Fi Wireless networking technology Ethernet Common wired networking technology

docs.title: 30. Exercise — Trace a Network Request
docs.text:
Choose a website or application you use regularly.

For example:

Your company's analytics application

Now try to trace a request.

Fill in:

Question Your Answer What is the client? What network is the client connected to? Is the connection wired or wireless? What device connects the local network to other networks? What domain name does the application use? What does DNS do? What server receives the request? Does the application need a database? Where is the data stored?

Then draw your own simplified architecture:

User → ______ → ______ → ______ → ______ → Data

Try to identify the role of every component.

docs.title: 31. Challenge Exercise — Explain It to a Non-Technical Person
docs.text:
Imagine someone asks:

"What happens when I open a website?"

Explain it without using technical jargon initially.

Then explain it again using at least these terms:

  • Client
  • Network
  • Router
  • DNS
  • IP address
  • Web server
  • Database
  • HTTPS

The goal isn't to memorize definitions.

The goal is to understand how the concepts interact.

docs.text:

Networks allow the components of an IT system to communicate.

Topic
docs.text: How IT Systems Store, Organize, Retrieve, and Exchange Data

docs.title: Day 5 Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

  1. Explain the difference between data and information.
  2. Explain why organizations treat data as an important asset.
  3. Explain what a database is.
  4. Explain what a relational database is.
  5. Identify tables, rows, columns, and fields.
  6. Explain primary keys.
